content:
It looks quite interesting. The latest ChatGPT update includes Mac integration: users can handle conversations directly within the Apple Messages app. This feature supports iMessage, SMS and RCS.

The Mac version of ChatGPT now has a new Apple Messages extension.

The new Apple Messages extension allows ChatGPT to read and search your chat history on Mac, as well as compose and send messages. OpenAI says this feature is available across all ChatGPT macOS desktop app plans and supports both ChatGPT and Codex.

Given the broad scope of permissions involved, the feature naturally raises concerns about privacy and control. OpenAI emphasises that sending messages requires user approval by default. Users should think carefully before granting permanent approval. OpenAI's extension guidelines detail the associated risks, explain how to revoke permissions, and outline a known issue involving bypassing the approval prompt.

At this stage, the feature only works on Macs with Apple Silicon; Intel models are not supported.

If you ask ChatGPT to send a message on your behalf, the system will pop up a confirmation prompt before sending. You can also choose to skip this confirmation step within individual conversations.

Want to find this new feature in ChatGPT? The link below will take you directly to the Messages extension page for ChatGPT for Mac.

Collaborative website editing, conversation snapshot sharing and more

Although the Messages extension is the headline new feature for Apple users this time, this update also includes several other improvements. For example, pinned conversations can now sync between the ChatGPT desktop app and iOS, allowing users to access important conversations on both Mac and iPhone at any time.

ChatGPT also now lets users share read-only local Codex conversation snapshots. Even if the original conversation is updated later, these snapshots will not change.

Links generated from personal accounts can be opened by anyone who has the URL; however, workspace links can only be opened by members of that workspace. OpenAI says Codex will mask known sensitive formats, but reminds users to check their own snapshots, as they may still contain sensitive information.

In addition, website owners can invite existing members within the same workspace to collaboratively edit websites with collaboration features enabled. After the owner completes the initial publication, editors can update content and database data, save versions, and publish updates. The owner retains control over access permissions, settings, analytics data and version rollback.

Some website owners can also change URLs hosted by ChatGPT without redeploying, and old addresses will automatically redirect to the new addresses.

Finally, the computer use history feature launched last week is now expanding to Pro, Business and Enterprise users in the European Economic Area, Switzerland and the UK. This opt-in feature requires the memory feature to be enabled first in order to work, and is off by default.

You can see the full launch announcement for this update here.
